claims.text: An adaptive machine-learning free-energy integration scheme can capture the free-energy landscapes of both solid and fluid states.
The proposed scheme will retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Selective sampling by active learning will reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD while maintaining predictive fidelity.
The target systems are multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting, considered in both solid and fluid phases.
Sparse-grid integration and active learning can identify the configurations most critical to free-energy integration.
A limited number of ab initio snapshots can replace exhaustive molecular-dynamics sampling.
The method is expected to apply from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature.
The method should first be validated on elemental and binary systems before extension to multicomponent alloys.
Targeted ab initio snapshots can transmit vibrational entropy, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling to the ML surrogate.
Active learning identifies phase-space regions where free-energy gradients are critical.
An ML surrogate trained on sparse but representative ab initio data can predict free-energy corrections.
Retaining the detailed physics through the surrogate will permit correct phase-free-energy calculations with fewer costly molecular-dynamics steps.
The proposed method will have free-energy and phase-property fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will be three to five times faster than TOR-TILD.
The anticipated speed advantage will be particularly pronounced in high-dimensional multicomponent systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluation and TOR-TILD on elemental and binary systems are the relevant baselines.
The method is intended for fusion transitions in elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Speed and fidelity may vary in highly anharmonic or strongly electron-coupled systems.
A deviation greater than 5% in phase free-energy differences or fusion temperature relative to converged ab initio molecular dynamics would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to achieve a significant speedup over TOR-TILD would falsify the hypothesis.
